Saulder, D. Schlegel, M. Schubnell, H. Seo, J. Silber, G. Tarl\'e, B. A. Weaver, C. Y\`eche, R. Zhou

papers.title: Primordial black holes forming during kination: the trapped, the overdense, and the void
papers.summary: We study primordial black-hole (PBH) formation in a single-field model which passes from slow roll, through a transient ultra-slow-roll phase, into kination. Nonlinear numerical-relativity simulations are used to follow localised, initially sub-Hubble field fluctuations across the non-attractor transition, to determine the resulting super-Hubble curvature profiles, and subsequently to evolve their re-entry during kination. Within the set of initial configurations explored here, we find three qualitatively distinct outcomes, namely a patch which remains trapped in inflation, a positive-curvature overdensity, and a negative-curvature void bounded by an overdense shell. Each may form a PBH, although by a different physical mechanism. For one selected profile in each of the overdense and void channels, we measure collapse thresholds and compare them with thresholds for sinc profiles. The comparison shows that neither the central curvature nor the peak linear compaction alone provides a profile- or channel-independent collapse criterion. PBH abundances in non-attractor models must therefore be formulated in terms of the distribution of complete profiles, with the trapped, overdense, and void channels treated separately.

authors.name: Cristian Joana

papers.title: Probing the baryonic--dark matter connection in galaxy clusters using X-rays with gated recurrent unit neural networks
papers.summary: Accurate cluster mass measurements are crucial for cosmology, yet conventional hydrostatic equilibrium (HSE) methods can suffer from systematic biases, particularly in dynamically disturbed systems. We present a gated recurrent unit (GRU) based deep learning framework for predicting three-dimensional mass profiles of galaxy clusters from spherically averaged intra-cluster medium (ICM) radial profiles. By treating ICM profiles as sequential data, the GRU captures radial dependencies and naturally handles profiles with different radial samplings. We train and validate the model using high-resolution hydrodynamical simulations from The Three Hundred Project, achieving unbiased mass predictions with a typical 1$\sigma$ scatter of $\sim$5% over most of the cluster region, significantly improving upon HSE estimates. The model provides radius-dependent uncertainty estimates and remains robust against variations in data quality and cluster morphology. When trained jointly on independent simulation suites (GIZMO-SIMBA and GADGET-X), it successfully generalises across both simulations. Feature importance analysis shows that enclosed gas mass is the dominant predictor, with pressure and temperature providing additional information on the radial mass distribution. We further apply the GRU model to X-ray observations of the REXCESS and X-COP cluster samples from XMM-Newton and compare the inferred mass profiles with HSE estimates. The GRU and HSE mass estimates show close agreement for the lower-mass REXCESS sample, while HSE masses are systematically lower than the GRU predictions for the higher-mass X-COP sample, an offset consistent with hydrostatic mass bias. This work provides a data-driven framework for cluster mass inference that bridges simulations and observations and can be extended to multi-wavelength datasets, including Sunyaev-Zel'dovich and optical observations.

authors.name: Asif Iqbal, Subhabrata Majumdar, Weiguang Cui, Elena Rasia, Gabriel W. Pratt, Daniel de Andres

papers.title: Emulating the complex galactic-scale orbital dynamics of LISA massive black hole pairs with normalizing flows
papers.summary: Massive black hole (MBH) pairs, formed in galaxy mergers, may coalesce in a burst of gravitational waves (GWs). Estimating the coalescence time-scales and rates is a long-standing astrophysical problem, essential to inform predictions for future GW detectors such as the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, but remains challenging: MBH orbital decay in realistic galactic environments is complex and stochastic, and non-axisymmetric structures such as stellar bars can perturb MBH pair dynamics, delaying or accelerating binary formation and undermining the assumption that dynamical friction alone sets the inspiral duration. Capturing this evolution requires simulations too expensive to run at population scale. Here we present an artificial intelligence framework that emulates the galactic-scale orbital decay of an inspiralling MBH using conditional normalizing flows trained on a large suite of semi-analytical orbital integrations. Our model captures the evolution of secondary MBHs orbiting within multi-component galactic merger remnants featuring rotating stellar discs and bars, across a broad range of MBH masses, orbital configurations, and bar properties. The trained emulator reproduces the simulations' decay-time distributions while reducing computational cost by orders of magnitude. For the first time, we apply this model to galaxy populations drawn from a cosmological simulation, exploiting morphological information on barred and non-barred galaxies to infer MBH binary formation time-scales across cosmic time. Our results show that stellar bars can alter the distribution of MBH binary formation times. More broadly, this demonstrates how simulation-based, surrogate machine learning emulators can unlock a class of astrophysical problems where the physics is well understood system-by-system but intractable at scale.

authors.name: Pedro R. Capelo, Carlos Moreno Martinez, Nodens Koren, Tommaso Zana, Elisa Bortolas, Matteo Bonetti, Janis Fluri, Thomas Hofmann, Lucio Mayer

papers.title: Single Frequency CMB Foreground Removal with Inter-scale Machine Learning
papers.summary: Accurate measurements of Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) B-mode polarization, a key probe of inflationary physics, are hindered by complex Galactic dust foregrounds. Traditional foreground removal with Internal Linear Combination (ILC) fully preserves the primordial signal but requires multi-frequency data and is limited to two-point statistics. We present a novel way to estimate and remove foregrounds at single frequency using signal-preserving machine learning that leverages inter-scale correlations. Using the DustFilaments simulations, we train CNNs to reconstruct large-scale foregrounds ($\ell 200$). We quantify the effectiveness of foreground removal with the residual foreground power, $f_{\rm{resid}}$, which gives the fraction of foreground power remaining after removal. Predictions using only small-scale $B$-modes achieve $f_{\rm{resid}}\simeq 0.704$, while adding temperature and $E$-modes decreases it to $f_{\rm{resid}} \simeq 0.376$. These results are still higher than the spatial ILC, which leverages multi-frequency data at Simons-Observatory-like frequencies. However, a hybrid network that uses both multi-frequency and inter-scale correlations attains $f_{\rm{resid}}=4.71\times10^{-4}$ when using $B$-mode inputs alone, and $3.62\times10^{-4}$ when using temperature and $E/B$-mode inputs. This network achieves a residual power of $\sim 7\times$ lower than ILC, while inheriting ILC's signal-preserving property. This is $\sim 2$--$3\times$ lower than a network that only uses multi-frequency inputs, demonstrating that correlations across scale are not redundant with correlations across frequency and that our techniques are complementary to multi-frequency foreground removal. However, this is achieved only for DustFilments and network generalization across simulations remains a key challenge for robust ML-based foreground removal. (abridged)

authors.name: Helen Shao, Fiona McCarthy, Blake D. Sherwin, Miles Cranmer, Carlos Hervias-Caimapo

papers.title: On an empirical method to build near-equilibrium axisymmetric and triaxial galaxy models
papers.summary: We present a numerical technique to implement $N$-body realizations of axisymmetric and triax- ial self-gravitating system starting from a spherical self-consistent models for which a phase-space distribution is known. The method builds up on the so-called adiabatic squeezing technique by K. Holley-Bockelmann et al. (2001) and ideally allows to control the effective ellipticities of the particle distribution. We discuss some preliminary tests and sketch a possible improvement of our method

authors.name: Pierfrancesco Di Cintio, Alessandro Alberto Trani, Valentina Cesare

papers.title: Using High-Resolution Spectroscopy to Study the Composition, Temperature, and Dynamics of Exoplanet Atmospheres
papers.summary: High-resolution spectroscopy, typically operating at resolving powers R greater or equal to 25,000, has matured into one of the primary techniques for characterising the atmospheres of extrasolar planets. The ability of HRS to resolve individual rotational-vibrational lines of molecular bands, combined with the large Doppler shifts experienced by close-in planets during their orbits, allows planetary signals to be separated from quasi-stationary telluric and stellar contamination. Since the pioneering detection of carbon monoxide in the transmission spectrum of HD 209458b, HRS has enabled the identification of more than a dozen chemical species, including H2O, CH4, HCN, TiO, VO, Na, K, Li, H-alpha, He I, Mg, Ca, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, and Ti, in a wide variety of transiting, non-transiting and directly imaged exoplanets . In addition to chemical abundances, HRS constrains the vertical temperature structure through the pressure dependence of line depths, and reveals atmospheric dynamics through Doppler shifts and asymmetries imprinted on the planetary cross-correlation function. This review synthesises observational and methodological progress from the past fifteen years with a focus on how current and forthcoming high-resolution facilities HARPS, ESPRESSO, NIRPS, CARMENES, CRIRES+, SPIRou, GIANO, and ultimately the ANDES, METIS and HARMONI instruments on the Extremely Large Telescope are reshaping our empirical view of exoplanet atmospheres.

authors.name: Mu'allim Yakubu

papers.title: Structural quasi-universality in highly magnetized differentially rotating neutron stars
papers.summary: Universal relations among macroscopic properties of neutron stars provide a powerful framework to probe their internal structures while minimizing uncertainties associated with the equation of state (EoS). Although such relations have been extensively studied for uniformly rotating stars, their extension to differentially rotating and strongly magnetized configurations is relatively less explored. We systematically investigate equilibrium configurations for a wide range of EoSs, rotation profiles, and magnetic field strengths with XNS numerical simulation code. For sequences with fixed angular momentum, we analyze the dependence of normalized moment of inertia on compactness. We establish a generalized quasi-universal relation between the moment of inertia and compactness that remains remarkably insensitive to the underlying EoS across uniformly rotating, differentially rotating, and strongly magnetized toroidal configurations. For sequences with fixed angular momentum, the normalized moment of inertia exhibits a quasi-universal dependence on compactness, with deviations primarily due to magnetic field strength and degree of differential rotation. We derive analytic expressions for these dependencies, enabling a unified phenomenological model applicable over a wide range of stellar configurations. As astrophysical applications, we quantify the systematic bias in magnetar luminosity estimates and the rotational kinetic energy of post-merger remnant of GW170817. These results extend quasi-universal relations beyond the standard assumptions of uniform rotation and weak magnetization, providing a robust framework for interpreting observations of highly magnetized and differentially rotating neutron stars, and enabling more reliable constraints on their astrophysical properties.

authors.name: Pratul Manna, Surajit Kalita

papers.title: X-ray Reflection as Diagnostic of Supermassive Black Hole Binary Properties
papers.summary: We investigate correlations between prominent features in the relativistic X-ray reflection spectrum emitted by an accreting supermassive black hole (SMBH) binary with the underlying properties of the binary system. Model-independent measurements of the relativistic Fe K$\alpha$ line ($\sim$6.4 keV) and the Compton reflection hump ($\sim$20-30 keV) are shown to be useful in constraining binary parameters. We compute 24,570 X-ray reflection spectra from two mini-disks attached to SMBHs at a fixed separation of 100 $GM/c^2$ on circular orbits, by varying its mass ratio, spin parameters, inclination, orbital phase and total mass accretion rate. We find that the location of the blue peak in the relativistic Fe K$\alpha$ is a relatively robust diagnostic of the binary inclination, which could be obtained from a single-epoch X-ray spectrum. Given a few epochs of spectra, one may be able to determine the orbital phase of the binary and place constraints on its mass ratio by monitoring the Fe K$\alpha$ centroid. Of all parameters, SMBH spin effects are most subtle and prone to measurement degeneracies. Some markers of high SMBH spin may nevertheless surface in the composite spectrum due to increased radiative efficiency. The approach developed here can be used to place preliminary constraints on binary parameters before a full parametrized X-ray spectral fitting method is available. It complements gravitational wave measurements by the Pulsar Timing Arrays (PTAs) and the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna by providing independent constraints on binary parameters that may be prone to degeneracy (inclination), or otherwise inaccessible (spin for PTAs).

authors.name: Julie Malewicz, Tamara Bogdanovi\'c, David R. Ballantyne, Laura Brenneman, Thomas Dauser

papers.title: Optical Signatures of Sgr A* and M87* with Dark Matter Halos
papers.summary: The event horizon telescope (EHT) has opened a new window onto the strong-field regime by imaging the shadows of the supermassive black holes (SMBHs) Sgr A* and M87*. These observations provide a unique laboratory for probing the dark matter (DM) distribution around black holes. In this work we systematically investigate the imprints of two distinct DM halo models, the cold DM (CDM), and the cored scalar field DM (SFDM) profiles on the gravitational lensing signatures of Sgr A* and M87*. We compute the photon spheres, shadows, weak and strong lensing observables, and caustic structures for both models. We then compared the obtained values of the shadow diameters with the EHT data, using $\chi^2$ statistics. We found that all the models are within $1.2\sigma$ of the measured shadow diameters with the small $\chi^2$ differences, $\Delta\chi^2 \lesssim 1.2$. The caustic analysis reveals distinct topological regimes, Sgr A* retains both tangential and radial critical curves, while M87* may show only tangential critical curves due to its larger mass. This topological difference provides a clear observational signature for future observations.

authors.name: Noraiz Tahir, Muhammad Ali Paracha, Mubasher Jamil

papers.title: [CII] as a global cold gas tracer in novel hydrodynamical simulations
papers.summary: [CII] emission is a powerful tool for studying the gas content in galaxies, especially at early stages of evolution. Given its low excitation potential, the [CII] 158 \mu m line is the main coolant of neutral gas in photodissociation regions and giant molecular clouds, hence a tracer of all phases of the interstellar medium. However, there is no consensus on what is the nature of the gas traced by this emission. We aim to provide insights into the physics of the [CII] emission and predictions for future observations. We used four pre-prepared simulations performed with a version of p-gadget-3, which includes the krome chemistry package. We implemented a postprocessing semi-analytical model to simulate the [CII] emission. We analysed an isolated Milky Way-mass-size galaxy, and three merger configurations: a co-rotating, counter-rotating, and perpendicular major mergers of two Milky Way-mass-size galaxies. We reproduce fundamental relations such as the [CII] luminosity and the star formation rate, L[CII]-SFR relation, in which mergers show an extra component for the [CII] emission not traced by the star formation alone. During quiescent or starburst stages, galaxies deviate from the L[CII]-SFR relation. We find that [CII] is a robust tracer of molecular gas, as well as atomic gas in both cold and warm phases on a global scale. Our results indicate that around 50 per cent of the total [CII] emission is traced by molecular gas, while 30 to 40 per cent is traced by atomic and ionised hydrogen regardless of the configuration. Our findings suggest that the nature of the [CII] emission depends strongly on the evolutionary history of galaxies, in which mergers and starbursts act as more efficient drivers of [CII] emission through collision with molecular hydrogen.

authors.name: Valentina P. Miranda, Patricia B. Tissera, Jorge Gonz\'alez-L\'opez, Emanuel Sillero

papers.title: Magnesium silicate condensation in sub-Neptune envelopes: the fundamental link between chemistry, structure, and observables
papers.summary: Chemical interactions between the hydrogen-dominated envelopes and silicate-rich interiors of sub-Neptunes likely play a key role in shaping their atmospheric structure, mass-radius relations, and upper atmosphere composition. While atmospheric abundances and structure deeply influence each other, many existing models have either considered the effects of chemical interactions without the structural implications or have modeled the envelope structure using oversimplified chemical networks. In this work, we introduce Rocky Raccoon, a coupled chemical equilibrium-atmospheric structure model. This model incorporates Mg, Si, O, C, and H species and produces self-consistent atmospheric chemical and thermal profiles for sub-Neptune envelopes, treating multi-species condensation for the first time. We find that the condensation sequence of magnesium silicates above a magma ocean is determined by the basal magma composition. We show that these condensation sequences drive the upper atmospheric composition to two endmembers: high oxygen abundances in the underlying melt produce compositions rich in oxygen-bearing volatiles (sub-solar C/O) and higher mean molecular weight atmospheres with $\mu \sim 4$ amu, while oxygen-poor melts produce lower mean molecular weight atmospheres dominated by methane and silane (super-solar C/O). The transition between the two regimes is abrupt and depends on melt properties like Mg/Si ratios and oxygen abundances. The different condensation sequences also lead to different thermal profiles, as deep convection is inhibited over different regions due to varying molecular weight gradients. Further experiments and simulations are key to resolving critical uncertainties in the condensation sequences and the corresponding significant impacts on sub-Neptune composition and thermal structure.

authors.name: William Misener, Peter Gao, Nicole L. Wallack, Maggie A. Thompson, Anat Shahar

papers.title: Filament-Arm Node Systems (FANS): A new probe of the winding and chirality of the cosmic web
papers.summary: We define Filament-Arm Node Systems (FANS), a new class of cosmic-web objects consisting of multiple filament arms connected to a common node, and use their geometry to construct an object-based test of cosmic chirality. With the cosmic-web node providing a natural reference point, FANS span characteristic scales of ~60 Mpc/h, allowing the coherent winding of their arms around the node to be measured directly. We define cosmic spirality as the amplitude of this winding and handedness as its signed clockwise (CW) or counter-clockwise (CCW) sense. We further introduce an axis-conditioned extrinsic estimator that searches for the projected signature of a coherent three-dimensional axial pattern of the handedness field, corresponding to a preferred axis of winding. Applying these measurements to two distinct SDSS filament reconstructions, and assessing their significance with sign-flip nulls and 27 controlled variations of the FANS construction parameters, we find no significant preference for CW or CCW winding, either globally or around a preferred axis. The data are therefore consistent with parity symmetry, as expected in standard LCDM cosmology. Comparing the lowest- and highest-redshift bins over 0.1<z<0.6, we find that cosmic spirality decreases with cosmic time, a trend that also persists within individual arm-multiplicity classes and may reflect the gravitational straightening of filament arms. These first constraints establish FANS as a new probe of cosmic-web symmetry and large-scale morphology and provide a baseline for future parity tests with the much larger filament samples expected from upcoming surveys.

authors.name: Pedro da Silveira Ferreira, Renyue Cen

papers.title: A Quantitative Method to Investigate the Spectral Class Time Evolution of Novae
papers.summary: Novae are spectroscopically classified as Fe II or He/N according to the dominance of Fe II, or He and N emission lines in their pre-nebular spectra, while spectra exhibiting both are classified as hybrid. Whereas the spectral class of a nova is known to correlate with its progenitor properties, a recent detailed spectroscopic follow-up of ten novae suggests instead a time evolution from "early He/N" to "Fe II" and to "late He/N". We investigate here this apparent contradiction using a spectroscopic dataset of 26 novae from the Astronomical Ring for Amateur Spectroscopy (ARAS) Database. For this purpose we introduce a quantitative coefficient, $\kappa$, defined as the ratio of the flux of the Fe II $\lambda$5169 line to the mean flux of five He and N emission lines, with $\kappa > 1$ indicating Fe II-dominated spectra and $\kappa < 1$ indicating He/N-dominated spectra. This coefficient is shown to provide a reliable quantitative tool for tracing nova spectral evolution while reducing biases from incomplete coverage. A significant fraction of the novae in our sample exhibit at least one transition between Fe II- and He/N-dominated phases. The time evolution of $\kappa$ closely follows their optical light-curves, repeatedly crossing unity in novae exhibiting jitters, which reveal non-monotonic spectral evolution. Since the light-curve shapes and their time-scales depend on intrinsic progenitor properties, particularly white dwarf mass, they also determine the duration of Fe II- and He/N-dominated phases, introducing a bias in spectral classification when it relies on early, sparse spectra.

authors.name: Maria Kopsacheili, Martin Guerrero, Diego Alejandro Vasquez Torres

papers.title: A Brief Review on the Statistical Properties of Fast Radio Bursts
papers.summary: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are millisecond-duration radio transients of extragalactic origin, whose emission mechanisms and progenitors remain unresolved. Statistical analyses of the rapidly growing samples provide a promising means to constrain the underlying physics. In this review, we synthesize the statistical properties derived from current FRB catalogs, encompassing constraints on dispersion measure, redshift, energy/luminosity functions, repetition rate, and host-galaxy demographics. For repeating FRBs, we examine the statistics of energy, fluence/flux, waiting time, and discuss time-series analyses that reveal memory effects and chaotic dynamics. We further discuss the observational discovery and theoretical interpretation of periodic activity, and survey polarization properties that probe the magneto-ionic environments of FRB sources. Throughout, we emphasize robust empirical trends, account for observational biases and selection effects, and outline outstanding open questions regarding the physical origin of these enigmatic bursts.

authors.name: Yu Sang, Hai-Nan Lin

papers.title: Diverse Metallicities in Protoclusters at $z \sim 3.4$ detected by Deep Learning
papers.summary: We present spectroscopic follow-up observations with Subaru/MOIRCS of four protocluster candidate regions identified by the deep-learning model PCFNet. In three candidate regions, we confirm four protoclusters at $z =$ 3.316, 3.403, 3.408 and 3.425, exhibiting galaxy density peaks over five times the uniform distribution. The detection rate of confirmed members aligns with PCFNet's predictions, underscoring its effectiveness. Analysis of spectral energy distributions (SEDs), incorporating up to ten photometric bands $(uu^*grizyJHK)$, reveals that protocluster members lie on the star-formation main sequence. The masses of the most massive halos in the protoclusters are estimated from the most massive stellar mass of the member galaxies, yielding $\log M_\mathrm{halo}/M_\odot=12.4$-$12.8$, which are consistent with those at this redshift predicted by cosmological simulations and are comparable to those of the progenitors of typical local clusters ($M_\mathrm{halo}^{z=0}\sim10^{14}M_\odot$). Using the Voronoi Tessellation Monte Carlo technique based on the probability of protocluster membership from PCFNet, we find that our protoclusters exhibit a significantly higher SFRD than the cosmic SFRD at $z\sim3.4$. Based on the [Oiii]/H$\beta$ emission line ratio, two protoclusters show marginally ($1.4$-$2\sigma$) higher average metallicities than the field, while the other protoclusters are statistically consistent with the field. These diverse metallicities highlight the environmental impact within protoclusters detected by PCFNet, likely reflecting the complex opposing interplay between metal-rich gas recycling and metal-poor gas inflow, which may depend on the surrounding environment of each protocluster. This work demonstrates PCFNet's capability to unveil diverse samples of high-redshift protoclusters, paving the way for a more comprehensive understanding of their role in galaxy evolution.

authors.name: Yoshihiro Takeda, Nobunari Kashikawa, Kei Ito, Jun Toshikawa, Mariko Kubo, Rieko Momose, Yongming Liang, Takehiro Yoshioka, Junya Arita, Hiroki Hoshi, Shunta Shimizu, Hisakazu Uchiyama, Satoshi Kikuta, Ryo Emori, Kentaro Koretomo

papers.title: Lensing in the Blue IV: The First Weak Gravitational Lensing Maps from the Stratosphere
papers.summary: The Super-Pressure Balloon-borne Imaging Telescope (SuperBIT) completed its science flight in April 2023, obtaining imaging data for 30 galaxy clusters. In this work, we present the first weak-lensing convergence maps from these observations, using six clusters selected from the 30 targets. We construct background-galaxy catalogs using SuperBIT's three-band photometry and a color-color-based method to separate foreground and background galaxies. Using the calibrated shapes of the selected background galaxies, we reconstruct the weak-lensing convergence field through Kaiser--Squires inversion. We compare the convergence signal-to-noise maps for the six clusters with independent tracers of the mass distribution, namely, red-sequence cluster-member number density maps. These results demonstrate the first successful reconstruction of a weak-lensing signal using imaging data from a sub-orbital astronomical observatory.

authors.name: Sayan Saha, Maya Amit, Jacqueline E. McCleary, Georgios N. Vassilakis, Emaad Paracha, Giulia Cerini, Spencer W. Everett, Leila Ohashi, Eric M. Huff, Gavin Leroy, Leo W. H. Fung, Richard Massey, Steven J. Benton, William C. Jones, Thuy Vy T. Luu, Ajay S. Gill, Mohamed M. Shaaban, Philippe Voyer, Adam Field, Adam Aoua, Anthony M. Brown, Paul Clark, Matthew Craigie, Christopher J. Damaren, Tim Eifler, David Harvey, Eric Habjan, John W. Hartley, Bradley Holder, Mathilde Jauzac, David Lagattuta, Jason S. -Y. Leung, Lun Li, Johanna M. Nagy, C. Barth Netterfield, Susan F. Redmond, Jason D. Rhodes, Andrew Robertson, L. Javier Romualdez, J\"urgen Schmoll, Ellen Sirks, Sut Ieng Tam, Karuna Tarafdar, Andr\'e Z. Vitorelli, Alfredo Zenteno

papers.title: Axial-Dipole and Equatorial-Dipole Coronal Holes: Congruent Magnetic Geometry, Divergent Evolution
papers.summary: While the Sun's polar fields reverse, the axial dipole is weak and low-latitude coronal holes are common. Where the equatorial dipole is strong, these holes form at its magnetic poles, as the axial-dipole coronal holes (ADCHs) of solar minimum form at the poles of the axial dipole; we call them equatorial-dipole coronal holes (EDCHs). Not every low-latitude hole is an EDCH: in 2024 August, near maximum, the quadrupole and higher multipoles led the field. Parker Solar Probe found fast wind from an EDCH deeply sub-Alfv\'enic at $9.9\,R_\odot$, at only $60\%$ of an asymptotic speed equal to that of polar wind, which is thought to accelerate faster. We ask whether coronal structure predicts this, using potential-field models of synthetic and observed fields. Pure axial and equatorial dipoles are exactly congruent, so any difference between the two classes must come from their orientation relative to differential rotation or from the surrounding multipoles. ADCHs are stationary and sustained by converging meridional flow. EDCHs depend on an equatorial dipole that active-region emergence builds and flux transport removes: over $18$-day sequences the axial dipole at minimum is steady to $1\%$, whereas the equatorial dipole varies by $21\%$ at maximum and $8\%$ in the declining phase. Most open flux in EDCHs expands less than in ADCHs, and their boundaries are dominated by pseudostreamers with non-monotonic expansion. Magnetic geometry alone does not predict slower acceleration from EDCHs; a real difference would point to extended heating by Alfv\'en-wave turbulence, which potential-field models cannot capture.

authors.name: Olga A. Panasenco, Yi-Ming Wang, Samuel T. Badman, Adam J. Finley, Yeimy J. Rivera

papers.title: When, Why, and How CMB Compression Fails
papers.summary: We test when compressed CMB likelihoods can be reliably used to constrain new physics beyond $\Lambda$CDM, formulating concrete criteria for when, why, and how CMB compression fails. We derive our conclusions by exploring a broad set of models that modify different aspects of the cosmological evolution, including late-time dark-energy dynamics, non-standard late-time dark-matter evolution through interactions or decay, and dark-matter models with persistently non-standard redshift evolution. For each case, we compare the results obtained from data combinations based on the full Planck-CMB likelihood with their counterparts based on a compressed CMB likelihood calibrated in $\Lambda$CDM. We find that the compression remains accurate for late-time dark-energy extensions that preserve the dark-matter background evolution and do not introduce significant additional perturbative effects. By contrast, modifying the dark-matter evolution breaks the mapping between the present-day matter density and the matter density at the epochs relevant to the CMB, causing the compressed constraints to fail even when the modification acts exclusively at late times. In these cases, the compressed likelihood can drastically alter the geometry of the multidimensional posterior distributions, shifting their centers, producing strongly anisotropic deformations, reordering principal modes, and generating genuine mixing and rotation of their eigendirections. These multidimensional distortions propagate into substantially incorrect marginalized constraints on cosmological parameters, with differences between the full and compressed analyses reaching nearly an order of magnitude in some of the cases studied here.

authors.name: Davide Pedrotti, William Giar\`e, Hanyu Cheng, Eleonora Di Valentino

papers.title: A strategy for astrometric quasar selection with Gaia DR3 and its application to discover new luminous $z>2$ quasars
papers.summary: We aim to provide a cookbook for purely astrometric selection of quasars with Gaia DR3 and to provide an example of its use for the identification of very luminous $z>2$ quasars. We analyse the Gaia DR3 astrometry of confirmed quasars and stationary sources. We show that the proper motion signal to noise $\mu/\sigma_{\mu}$ follows a Rayleigh-like distribution. We also show the importance of properly taking into account the correlation between proper motions in right ascension and declination, as well as the non-linear error propagation. We adopt the Mahalanobis distance to the null proper-motion hypothesis. A scaled $\chi^2$ distribution with $k=2$ and scale $s=1.1485$ is fitted to Gaia-CRF3; the corresponding $\pm2\sigma$ Gaussian-equivalent threshold is $D^2_{M(\mu)}2$ quasars without redshifts in the literature. Our proposed astrometric selection strategy recovers 95\% of known quasars. Its potential use for new discoveries is demonstrated by the identification of 24 very luminous $z>2$ quasars. Ten of these are new discoveries and for an additional seven we correct the redshifts determined by other methods.}

authors.name: J. Li, J. P. U. Fynbo

papers.title: High-frequency water megamasers as precision probes of black holes, galaxies and cosmology: A case for a next-generation sub-mm/mm interferometer
papers.summary: Water megamasers in the circumnuclear disks of active galactic nuclei are among the most precise probes of supermassive black holes. VLBI imaging of 22 GHz disk masers has provided geometric distances to independently constrain $H_0$, accurate black hole mass measurements, and sub-parsec views of accretion disk geometry. ALMA has opened a new window into water maser transitions in the sub-mm/mm regime, which trace temperatures, densities and disk regions that are inaccessible at 22 GHz, and can be observed at higher spatial resolution and with less free-free absorption. However, current detections are limited to a few bright extragalactic masers in nearby galaxies. We present the case for a next-generation sub-mm/mm interferometer - ALMA2040 - that would open a new parameter space for maser studies. We show that a 10-fold increase in line sensitivity and three times longer baselines compared to ALMA would transform sub-mm maser studies from a few bright detections into a population-level probe, delivering black hole masses and geometric distances from sub-mm masers alone, independent of and complementary to 22 GHz measurements. Integrated into a VLBI array, ALMA2040 would resolve maser disks out to $>$160 Mpc, extend maser black hole masses into the largely untested intermediate-mass regime, reveal magnetic field structure in accretion disks through polarization studies, and test systematics in $H_0$ measurements.

authors.name: Ingyin Zaw, C. M. Violette Impellizzeri, Dominic W. Pesce, Elizabeth Humphreys, Hannah R. Stacey, Sophie Venselaar, Chengyu Kuo, Jack Gallimore, Yoshiaki Hagiwara, Satoki Matsushita, Jim Braatz

papers.title: Gaia in Technicolor. I. A Simple Variability-Encoded Color-Magnitude Diagram
papers.summary: The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram is one of the most important tools in stellar astrophysics. In its modern, empirical form as the Gaia color-magnitude diagram (CMD), each star is represented with a point determined from its time-averaged brightness and color. However, many stars are intrinsically variable, and the fixed-point representation ignores the variety of ways in which a star can vary. As a system pulsates, eclipses, is irradiated, erupts, or otherwise varies, it moves through the CMD along a trajectory whose size, slope, and shape are determined by the physics driving the brightness and color variability. Here we exploit the near-simultaneous, three-band, multi-epoch photometry (MEP) released for ~11.7 million sources in Gaia DR3 to construct a variability-encoded CMD (VECMD). In this updated take on the traditional CMD, each star is represented not by a point but by a linear segment approximating the path it traces in absolute magnitude and color as it varies. Because these trajectories are built from the raw epoch data, they are agnostic to period and do not require phase-folding. We show that radial-mode pulsators trace looped, Lissajous-like trajectories that can encode the phase lag between radius and temperature. The Hertzsprung bump is even visible in the CMD loops of some Cepheids. Variable binary systems can trace tight color-correlated lines and/or hooked paths. Accreting and dust-obscured systems trace long, high-amplitude tracks aligned with the outburst or reddening vector. Distinct regions of the VECMD are dominated by distinct trajectory morphologies. We argue that these trajectories are period-independent fingerprints well suited to machine learning classification, which we will pursue on the much larger epoch-photometry sample expected in Gaia DR4. Finally, we present a free app called IVECMD for finding, classifying, and analyzing variable stars in the VECMD.

authors.name: Brad N. Barlow, Bennett C. Kirby

papers.title: Modeling Multi-band Active Galactic Nuclei Lightcurves Using a Self-supervised Attentive Neural Process Network
papers.summary: With the the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), observations of tens of millions of quasars are expected. We present a machine-learning framework based on an attentive neural process (ANP) that models stochastic quasar variability and jointly performs two tasks: (i) probabilistic reconstruction of quasar light curves in all six LSST bands, and (ii) inference of physical parameters of the AGN system --- black hole mass, Eddington ratio, and intrinsic variability timescale --- with joint, full-covariance posteriors. The model processes all six bands within a single masked attention mechanism, so that observations in any band constrain the shared driving process, and natively handles irregularly and asynchronously sampled light curves with realistic heteroscedastic noise. We train and evaluate on full ten-year light curves simulated with a relativistic accretion-disk reprocessing model, observed through the fielded Rubin baseline cadence with per-visit photometric noise. The light-curve model is trained with self-supervised, learning from the sparse noisy observations alone and never accessing the underlying noiseless light curves. On a held-out test set, we show that our ANP model reach comparable performances to that of the near-optimal baseline Gaussian process model, while exceeding it in power spectrum reconstruction and damped-random walk timescale estimation. The compact learned latent representation supports future downstream applications, and the fully observation-driven training objective enables direct fine-tuning on real LSST light curves.

authors.name: Tzuken Shen, Chengcheng Xin, Joshua Fagin, Ashley Villar, Matthew J. Graham, K. E. Saavik Ford

papers.title: OGLE-2013-BLG-1125/MOA-2013-BLG-584: Discovery of a gas giant orbiting an M dwarf
papers.summary: We report the discovery and characterization of a planetary system in the microlensing event OGLE-2013-BLG-1125/MOA-2013-BLG-584. We analyze photometric data from OGLE and MOA surveys, as well as LCO, $\mu$FUN, and Mindstep follow-up telescopes to model the microlensing light curve. We also used data from the Keck II telescope collected in 2018 to obtain additional constraints on the lensing system. We found a Saturn-mass planet of mass $M_{\rm p}=105\pm13 \ M_\oplus$ orbiting a low-mass host star $M_{\rm L}=0.139\pm0.011 \ M_\odot$ at $1.00\pm0.08$ kpc from Earth. This discovery adds to the small sample of giant planets orbiting low-mass stars and provides constraints on planet formation theories.

authors.name: E. Bachelet, M. Hundertmark, V. Bozza, J. -P. Beaulieu, A. Udalski

papers.title: pbhalo: computing primordial black hole and minihalo populations from a single primordial perturbation spectrum
papers.summary: An enhancement of the primordial curvature power spectrum on small scales can give rise to two populations of compact objects: primordial black holes (PBHs), which form during radiation domination, and dark matter minihalos, including ultracompact minihalos (UCMHs), which form from the same modes during matter domination. We present pbhalo, an open-source Python package that computes the PBH mass function, the halo mass function and the UCMH abundance from a single spectrum in a given cosmology and applies observational constraints on the PBH abundance and on the spectrum jointly. The package components are validated against colossus (a code for halo mass functions and cosmological quantities), pbhstat (a code for the PBH mass function from a given spectrum) and published results; joint constraints are illustrated for lognormal peaks. The code is distributed under the MIT license.

authors.name: Bogdan A. Rudenko

papers.title: Robust statistical significance for Gravitational Wave inference
papers.summary: The field of gravitational-wave data analysis heavily relies on Bayes factors to make astrophysical statements about detected signals. This is true on an event level, for example when discussing the potential detection of orbital precession or eccentricity, as well as on a population level. For the latter, a main limiting factor is the growing bias resulting from accumulating per-event uncertainties related to stochastic sampling. In both cases, the computational cost of calculating Bayes factors severely limits the astrophysical usefulness of the results: Though Bayes factors robustly quantify the data's preference towards one model, one cannot generally determine how likely an equally large value is to arise under the null hypothesis. This paper applies evidence networks, amortized neural estimators which can infer Bayes factors after learning the distinguishability between two datasets, to the aforementioned problems. This makes it possible to construct empirical Bayes factor distributions under different signal assumptions, providing a calibration between observation and discovery significance. Using simulated Gaussian noise, we apply this method to a search for orbital precession in gravitational-wave data and achieve compatible results to current state-of-the-art approaches that require stochastic sampling. We further show that high precision of the achieved results leads to recovering injected isotropic-spin population fractions without discernible bias for populations of up to $10^4$ events on a simplified example. More generally, because the method does not require explicit likelihood evaluations, this lays a clear path towards a likelihood-free framework that does not rely on the assumption of Gaussian and stationary noise.

authors.name: Alexandre S\'ebastien G\"ottel

papers.title: Stellar Bars Reshape the Spatial Distribution of UV-bright Clumps in Nearby Galaxies
papers.summary: Stellar bars redistribute gas and angular momentum in disk galaxies, but whether they mainly change the amount or the spatial organization of recent star formation remains uncertain. We use archival HST/WFC3 F275W imaging to study 70 barred galaxies and 95 unbarred control galaxies matched in stellar mass, optical color, redshift, and F275W background noise. A uniform dendrogram-based procedure identifies 95,486 UV-bright star-forming clumps. We compare their radial and azimuthal distributions, central F275W emission, and luminosity and size distribution functions. Relative to their controls, barred galaxies show a deficit of clumps at intermediate radii broadly corresponding to the bar region, followed by a local recovery near the bar ends. Their clumps are also preferentially concentrated along the bar major axis. These spatial differences are stronger in high-mass galaxies. Normalized bar length is more closely associated with the radial redistribution and central F275W concentration than bar ellipticity, although its relation to the azimuthal distribution is less uniform. When galactocentric radius is normalized by bar length, the recovery occurs near $R/R_{\rm bar}\sim1$, indicating that the bar sets a characteristic scale for the redistribution. Despite these spatial differences, barred and control galaxies have broadly similar clump luminosity and size distribution functions. Our results suggest that stellar bars mainly reorganize where recent star formation occurs, rather than substantially altering the observed luminosities and sizes of individual UV clumps, and that this effect depends on galaxy mass and bar extent.

authors.name: Zhimin Zhou, Jianfei Liu

papers.title: von Neumann Stability Analysis of Braginskii MHD: Thermal Conduction, Viscosity, Magnetic Diffusion, and Thermoelectric Effects; and an Implementation in Athena++
papers.summary: Athena++ is a finite-volume astrophysical magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) code. As of writing, isotropic thermal conduction and kinematic viscosity, Ohmic resistivity, and ambipolar diffusion are present in the main branch. Here we present a fork of Athena++, ``Athena-Aniso''. It implements fully anisotropic thermal conduction (parallel, perpendicular, and the Righi--Leduc effect); anisotropic viscosity (all five Braginskii viscosity tensors); the Hall effect; and several thermoelectric effects (Peltier, Seebeck, Nernst, and Ettingshausen). These effects can be weighted by ionisation fraction in a partially ionised gas, with the neutral part diffusing isotropically. We have also added isotropic bulk viscosity. The Biermann battery is not implemented here. The dissipative terms have super-time-stepping support, while the non-dissipative terms are combined with the ideal MHD flux. A CFL condition for all terms is derived and implemented using von Neumann stability analysis. The dissipative terms are found to be stable under first-order time integration. The non-dissipative terms are found to be stable under third-order time integration. We additionally derive new signal speeds for a modified HLLE Riemann solver. These suppress grid-scale non-linear instabilities still present in the non-dissipative terms. The Nernst/Ettingshausen system is found to be ill-posed unless it is stabilised by both perpendicular thermal conduction and perpendicular magnetic diffusion. We derive a well-posedness criterion for this. We provide numerical tests of each implemented effect against derived analytical solutions.

authors.name: Alexandra F. Albery, Julian M. Pittard

papers.title: Magnetically supramassive and hypermassive compact stars
papers.summary: It is known that the mass of a magnetized relativistic compact star is larger than that of non-magnetized one for the same equation of state and central density, albeit the excess of mass is sizable only if the magnetic fields are strong enough, B~10^17-10^18G. Using our recently developed numerical code COCAL, we systematically compute such compact star solutions in equilibrium associated with mixed poloidal and toroidal magnetic fields, and show the magnetically supramassive solutions whose masses exceed by more than 10% the maximum mass of the static and spherically symmetric solutions. For some extremely strong magnetic field configurations, we also obtain solutions more massive than the maximum mass of the uniformly rotating solutions at the Kepler (mass-shedding) limit, namely magnetically hypermassive solutions.

authors.name: Koji Uryu, Shijun Yoshida, Eric Gourgoulhon, Charalampos Markakis, Kotaro Fujisawa, Antonios Tsokaros, Keisuke Taniguchi, Mina Zamani, Lambros Boukas

papers.title: A System One Approach to General Protein Evolution
papers.summary: Protein engineering requires deciding which mutation to test next and when to stop. Existing approaches often require target-family measurements, encode candidates separately, or return scores that are not calibrated to the assay. We introduce Pev, a general mutation policy that explores a System One approach to protein evolution: learning from experiments across families to make decisions in a single parallel query. Given a parent sequence and an assay context, Pev encodes the parent once and returns calibrated probabilities for choosing an edit or stopping, together with each edit's probability of improving the assay outcome. One policy covers peptides, small folded domains, and antibodies across binding and stability objectives, without fitting model weights to the target family. In ten-well screens on held-out families, Pev finds 3.3$\times$ as many beneficial mutations as random selection and 1.8$\times$ as many as zero-shot ESM-2. It also outperforms a ridge surrogate refitted on target measurements in closed-loop search on the held-out GB1 landscape. Post-hoc calibration improves probability reliability without changing decisions, while shared encoding provides over 800$\times$ the throughput of per-mutant encoding at 1,000 candidates per request. These results suggest that a System One approach could support efficient experimental decisions across protein families, with Pev providing an initial demonstration.

authors.name: Yibo Wen, Han Liu

papers.title: AgentCount: An Agentic Workflow for Traceable Colony Counting and Insight Generation from Agar Plate Images
papers.summary: Colony counting is commonly used to evaluate microbial populations in food safety testing and microbiological studies. Despite its wide application, manual counting is time-consuming and operator-dependent, and the final count often lacks a record of the objects included in the measurement. To address these limitations, this study presents AgentCount, an open-source agentic workflow for colony counting and result interpretation from agar plate images. Plate photographs and plating metadata are processed through seven agents for image quality control, plate localisation, colony detection, counting, CFU calculation, validation, and reporting. Colony detection is performed using Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) with multiple text prompts and morphology-based filtering. After that, replicate statistics are calculated and a large language model (LLM)-based agent is used to generate a results narrative. Intermediate outputs, including quality scores, segmentation masks, detections, and warnings, are retained to support review of the reported values. The workflow also extends to skill-guided analysis of archived microbial population data. In a retrospective comparison with two previously published studies, we benchmarked 241 published endpoints, including all 216 mean +- SD values of the meat-analogue pathogen tables; on the 168 endpoints with a complete n=6 replicate source, 164 (97.6%) agreed within 0.01 log10 units. Overall, AgentCount demonstrates the promising potential of agentic workflows for applications in applied microbiology.

authors.name: Zhuosheng Liu, Austin E. Weber

papers.title: AcupunctureBench: A Multimodal Benchmark for Evaluating Generative Models in the Acupuncture Domain
papers.summary: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied in the field of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), standardized benchmark evaluations for TCM have gradually emerged. Acupuncture is a crucial component of TCM. However, existing evaluation benchmarks are lacking in this domain. To address this gap, this paper proposes AcupunctureBench, the first independently constructed large-scale multimodal benchmark for the acupuncture domain, covering text, image, and video modalities. The AcupunctureBench spans multidimen sional knowledge in acupuncture, including acupuncture theory, meridians and acupoints, clinical reasoning, TCM syndromes, and practical acupoint operation. To achieve large-scale construction while ensuring medical professionalism, this work designs a human-machine collaborative data construction pipeline and proposes efficient deduplication strategies to reduce redundant samples, while extensively adopting data synthesis to mitigate data leak age risks. AcupunctureBench contains a total of 58,526 question samples and 1,216 video samples, covering multiple task types including objective questions, subjective question answering, case analysis, image understanding, image reasoning, and video understanding. Based on this benchmark, this paper evaluates 14 large language models, 14 large multimodal models, and 4 video foundation models, and further releases the first dedicated evaluation website for the acupuncture domain.

authors.name: Shusheng Li, Yifei Qu, Zichen Han, Xingye Zhang, Zhongxin Wei, Yicheng Qiao, Jiaxin Shen, Changshuai Zhang, Siyuan Guo, Haiyan Ren, Xingfang Pan, Yangyang Liu, Zhaoshui He, Shuguo Hu, Wenjun Tan

papers.title: Deep-Learning Algorithm for Indeterminate Thyroid Nodules: Comparison and Combination with Molecular Testing
papers.summary: Thyroid nodules with indeterminate cytology (Bethesda III) carry an intermediate risk of malignancy, and molecular testing is widely used to decide between surgery and surveillance, but it is costly and not universally available. We investigated whether a convolutional neural network (CNN) applied to routine ultrasound images can stratify Bethesda III nodules, and how it compares and combines with molecular testing. We retrospectively identified 466 nodule records from 418 patients who underwent molecular testing (Afirma or ThyroSeq). A CNN pre-trained on determinate nodules was adapted to indeterminate nodules with soft labels and transfer learning. After removal of duplicate records, 119 nodules with surgical pathology were used for development and 47 were held out for testing. On the test set, the deep learning (DL) model achieved an AUC of 0.73 (95% CI 0.51-0.94), compared with 0.55 (0.38-0.71) for molecular testing (P = 0.15). At a cut-off inherited from the original algorithm, the DL model was more specific than molecular testing (0.95 vs 0.32; P < 0.001), with a higher positive predictive value (0.67 vs 0.21), a lower sensitivity (0.44 vs 0.78; P = 0.25) and a similar negative predictive value (0.88 vs 0.86). All six DL-positive test nodules were molecular-positive, and the DL output split the molecular-positive nodules into a high-risk (4/6 malignant) and a lower-risk group (3/27 malignant; P = 0.01). Surgical verification was strongly driven by the molecular result (99% of positive vs 19% of negative results), and molecular-test accuracy depended on the platform. A logistic regression of the DL output, nodule size and the molecular result dropped the DL term and did not improve on the DL output alone. Ultrasound DL complemented molecular testing for Bethesda III nodules, in particular by identifying molecular-positive nodules at lower risk of malignancy.

authors.name: Jichen Yang, Jeffrey Ashton, Jikai Zhang, Maciej A. Mazurowski, Benjamin Wildman-Tobriner

papers.title: A Training-Free Socket for DNA in Frozen Language Models
papers.summary: Connecting a DNA foundation model to a large language model (LLM) usually requires training a connector, and often the LLM too. We show that a closed-form map is enough for gene-level questions. Our method, the socket, fits one ridge regression (the plug) from frozen Evo 2 features to the host LLM's own representation of the gene's symbol, name, and description at an early layer. The plug's output replaces the hidden state at placeholder positions, and no gradient passes through the host. We test it on GeneHop, a five-way multiple-choice benchmark split by homology. In a single run on the held-out test set, under a frozen analysis plan, real DNA beats shuffled DNA on all four hosts: by +22.2 points [19.8, 25.0] on Qwen3.5-4B, +26.1 [24.3, 27.9] on Qwen3.6-27B, +16.7 [14.2, 19.7] on Mistral-7B, and +18.4 [16.2, 21.0] on OLMo-2-7B. All four survive Holm correction, every null control stays within two points of the sham level, and the development results agree within 2.3 points. A layer rule that uses no task items was selected on three hosts; it predicted the working layer of the fourth before any DNA-plug scoring on it. A text-only linear map lets one plug feed any other host, at a cost of at most 0.9 points on test. The socket conveys gene identity: nearest-neighbour retrieval recovers 72-84% of the effect, but the plug beats it on every host by 3.0-5.2 points and keeps most of its effect without training homologs.

authors.name: Arash Fatehi

papers.title: VenusGenome: Genome-Aware Masked Autoencoding for Microbial Genome Representation Learning
papers.summary: Genomic-context models have shown that contextualizing protein embeddings can improve predictions of microbial function. We observe that a gene's protein embedding is partially predictable from the embeddings of neighboring genes in the genome, motivating high-ratio masking that requires reconstruction from sparser genomic context. Genomic modeling must also distinguish biological relationships from assembly conventions, since the ordering of separate contigs does not imply adjacency and strand labels depend on the reference orientation. We therefore introduce VenusGenome, a gene-resolution masked autoencoder that combines visible-only encoding with genome-aware attention incorporating contig boundaries, relative strand orientations, and gene positions. We pretrain this model on a curated corpus of over 1.7 million microbial genome assemblies from isolate and metagenomic sources, using frozen protein embeddings as gene-level inputs. Across genome-level phenotype prediction and gene-level tasks, the resulting frozen representations achieve the highest mean performance among the evaluated models on nine of eleven primary metrics. An exploratory gene-input perturbation analysis further links representation sensitivity to experimentally measured fitness defects. Ablations support the contribution of genome-aware attention and show the benefits of masked autoencoding over BERT-style masked modeling, with further gains from higher masking ratios.

authors.name: Zhang Liang, Zhang Yukun, Tan Yang, Jiang Fan, Zhong Bozitao, Cheng Xiaoran, Hong Liang, Li Mingchen, Yu Yuanxi

papers.title: Rethinking One Gene, One Token: Transcriptome-Aware Tokenization for Single-Cell Foundation Models
papers.summary: Single-cell foundation models typically treat each gene as a token, which is both costly and wasteful. A cell can express thousands of genes, so one token per gene makes self-attention expensive, yet many of these genes are detected at low levels and carry too little signal to deserve a token of their own. Genes that are expressed together could instead share a token, leaving separate tokens for genes that stand out. We introduce scTAT (Transcriptome-Aware Tokenization), which pairs a gene-set vocabulary with a per-cell tokenizer. The vocabulary holds overlapping gene sets that recur with stable relative expression across the pretraining corpus. Using these sets raises two difficulties. First, which genes should share a token depends on the cell, whereas existing multi-gene tokens fix the grouping in advance. Second, gene sets of different sizes must be compared with single genes on a common scale. The tokenizer therefore decides per cell, letting gene sets and single genes compete for token positions under an expression score normalized by the square root of set size. Training still reconstructs individual genes, so predictions stay at gene resolution. In frozen-embedding cell-type annotation, scTAT matches the strongest one-gene-per-token model with half the token budget. Its advantage over one-gene-per-token models at the same budget grows as the budget shrinks and the tokenizer assigns more positions to gene sets. Encoding the same genes with gene-set tokens also nearly halves the Transformer's matrix-multiplication cost. These results show that a token need not hold exactly one gene: when the tokenizer decides per cell which genes share a token, a fixed budget covers more of each transcriptome at no cost in annotation accuracy.

authors.name: Jiaqi Xiong, Jiaying Li, Yu Zheng, Xiang Zhou, Ziteng Wang, Xinting Hu, Jiaxin Qi

papers.title: Morpheus.AI: agents autonomously generate, execute and refine virtual tissue models
papers.summary: Virtual tissue models link observations to mechanistic hypotheses, but building them demands expertise in biology, mathematics and programming. Here, large language model (LLM) agents paired with the simulator Morpheus (Morpheus.AI) autonomously built such models from fifteen benchmark studies, five without a published model. With a frontier LLM, agents that ran their simulations met 83-86% of study-specific criteria in under two hours and for under US\$4 per model. Such agents could make in silico modeling routine.

authors.name: Prerana Chandratre, Anjali Sharma, Justin B\"urger Michaelis, Diego Jahn, J\"orn Starru{\ss}, Lutz Brusch, Simon Syga

papers.title: BIOTRAM: Biochemistry-informed Transformer for Relative Abundance via Metabarcoding
papers.summary: Arthropod monitoring at scale begins with metabarcoding of bulk samples: trap collections of hundreds to thousands of specimens processed as one unit, extraction of DNA from the bulked specimens, then sequencing of the DNA from all specimens together. Metabarcoding reveals which taxa such a sample contains, but due to factors such as differing DNA amplification rates and body sizes, its read counts do not neatly correspond to how abundant the different taxa are relative to one another. This lack of relative abundance limits the data's utility for the multitude of ecological analyses that depend on it. We propose BIOTRAM: a neural network that estimates per-taxon specimen counts by dividing the observed read counts by a learned read yield per specimen, which it factors into the DNA each specimen contributes and how efficiently that DNA is amplified. On a paired dataset of 1,188 bottles (800 k specimens) processed both by metabarcoding and by comprehensive individual barcoding for ground-truthing, BIOTRAM reduces the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the estimated and the true composition from 0.3586 for raw read proportions (the usual proxy for abundance) to 0.1200. Trained on the same objective and inputs as four generic deep architectures, all with tuned loss weights, it reaches a count error 3.2% below that of the strongest of them and the lowest composition divergence. It also generalizes to out-of-domain data better, beating all baselines on bottles from unseen regions, later collection dates and unseen sequencing batches, and transferring to data from an unseen laboratory. Structuring the mapping from reads to counts around the steps of the experimental pipeline thus yields more accurate abundance estimates than leaving that mapping unconstrained.

Powell, Diego Inclan, Alice Calvente, David Dunson, Brian Fisher, Tomas Roslin, Otso Ovaskainen, Paul D. N. Hebert, Graham W. Taylor

papers.title: CellCanon: An Agentic Cellular World Model for Prediction, Explanation, and Observation-Driven Updating
papers.summary: Biological discovery requires using molecular knowledge and new measurements to infer responses beyond the conditions already observed. We introduce CellCanon, the first agentic cellular world model to unify single-cell expression prediction, evidence-grounded explanation, and observation-driven updating. Its predictive core reuses condition-level biological evidence across gene-specific numerical readouts to guide single-cell expression generation. A shared world state links predictions, acquired measurements, and source-linked claims, supporting explanation and revision. On 339 held-out SciPlex3 conditions across three cell lines, CellCanon improves differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 over the best baseline for each metric by 63.3% and 17.3%, respectively, and direction Macro-F1 by 7.2%. Relative to gene-wise reasoning on matched drug-cell cohorts, measured language-model token use falls by 99.77% for Predict and 98.41% for Explain. On the source-grounded benchmark, Explain correctly answers all answerable questions with supporting proofs and identifies all insufficient-evidence cases. In simulated experimental feedback, Update uses one measured source context per drug to exceed the best fine-tuned baselines in differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 without changing model weights. Together, these capabilities support a cumulative account of cellular responses, with predictions and biological judgments that can be revised as evidence accumulates.

authors.name: Zhaokang Liang, Shuyang Zhuang, Xiaoran Jiao, Hao Chen

papers.title: Can a self-sustaining chemical network emerge due to just a few catalysts?
papers.summary: Understanding how self-sustaining chemical reaction networks can emerge from simple molecules is an important question in chemical approaches to the origin of life. Reflexively autocatalytic and food-generated (RAF) sets provide a mathematical framework for investigating this question. This line of research goes back to the early work of Kauffman on autocatalytic reaction networks and was subsequently developed through the probabilistic framework of Mossel and Steel. Further contributions by Hordijk, Steel, and collaborators extended the theory to more heterogeneous forms of catalysis, including reaction-dependent probabilities or power-law distributions of catalytic activity. We introduce a stochastic model that combines heterogeneous molecular catalytic activity with reaction-dependent molecule-reaction compatibility. By assigning random catalytic weights to molecules and incorporating compatibility through an explicit formulation of catalysis probabilities, our model provides a concrete and flexible setting that captures both sources of heterogeneity while remaining mathematically tractable. We establish novel and general criteria for RAF formation and nonformation. We further demonstrate that classical phase-transition criteria need not remain valid in the presence of reaction-dependent catalysis. For heavy-tailed catalytic weights, we identify and rigorously quantify an additional phase transition. In models with finite-mean catalytic weights, RAF formation and nonformation are governed by a catalytic intensity parameter. For infinite-mean weights, however, we show that RAFs may emerge with probability tending to one even when the catalytic intensity parameter tends to zero.

authors.name: Jinsu Kim, Ercan S\"onmez

papers.title: A minimal E/I circuit model explains differential recovery from amblyopia under TTX and reverse occlusion
papers.summary: Recovery from amblyopia beyond the critical period remains a major challenge in visual neuroscience. Experimental studies show that transient inactivation of the fellow eye with tetrodotoxin (TTX) produces stronger and more persistent recovery than reverse occlusion (RO), despite both interventions reducing competition from the fellow eye. The circuit mechanisms underlying this difference remain unclear. We develop a minimal cortical circuit model combining excitatory-inhibitory population dynamics, BCM-like metaplasticity, homeostatic regulation, and eye-specific synaptic plasticity. Monocular deprivation drives the network into an amblyopic operating regime with reduced excitatory activity and fellow-eye dominance. Phase-plane and operating-regime analyses show that TTX and RO subsequently place the circuit in distinct dynamical states. TTX lowers inhibitory activity while maintaining excitatory activity above the BCM modification threshold, creating a larger plasticity-permissive regime than RO. These differences produce stronger recovery of amblyopic-eye responsiveness and greater correction of ocular dominance under TTX. A local robustness analysis across 300 perturbed parameter sets shows that the TTX advantage is not dependent on a narrowly tuned parameter choice. These results provide a mechanistic account of the differential efficacy of fellow-eye inactivation and suggest that recovery from sensory deprivation depends not only on changes in sensory input, but also on the dynamical operating regime of the cortical circuit.

authors.name: Lawrence Udeigwe

papers.title: Discrete Backbone Elasticity and Curvature-Dependent Torsion Statistics in Proteins
papers.summary: Coarse-grained models of protein conformational dynamics use $\mathrm{C}_\alpha$ geometry to describe the probabilities of regular helices, ordered turns and disordered conformations. To test how much of this order arises from local chain elasticity, we connect discrete Hasimoto frame transport to neighboring bending mismatch, deriving a curvature-product torsion interaction and a six-parameter generalized von Mises density. Fitted on 194 chains from the ATLAS molecular dynamics database and tested on 1744 sequence-nonredundant proteins, this baseline reduces negative log-density loss from 1.490 to 1.160 nats, torsion-sign error from 12.26 to 2.15 percentage points, and helix-fraction error from 21.84 to 10.41 points. Ablations and circular-moment projections against reference generative models motivate extensions to anisotropic stiffness and two partition-function-weighted elastic states, further lowering test loss to 0.790 nats and helix error to 1.65 points. The fixed hierarchy also improves predictions across 72 trajectories of peptides $\mathrm{Fs}$ and $(\mathrm{AAQAA})_3$ and miniprotein $\mathrm{HP35}$ spanning varied starting conformations and force fields. Remaining angular errors in these trajectories are associated with atomic context at shared bends, as bend-matched peptide frames adopt opposite torsion signs with distinct hydrogen-bond patterns and a proline-containing $\mathrm{HP35}$ turn remains at negative torsion. Introducing a bilinearly coupled $\mathrm{C}_\alpha$--$\mathrm{N}$ orientation angle largely reparameterizes the existing bend-dependent harmonics, with an empirical $L^2$ Gram projection placing 96.7\% to 99.6\% of its added coefficient-function squared norm within the original six-function span. These results link discrete Hasimoto elasticity to statistical backbone potentials and clarify the scope and limits of local $\mathrm{C}_\alpha$ geometry.

authors.name: Yiquan Wang, Mingyu Bian, Jiayuan Ma

papers.title: Mind Control of LLMs via Closed-Loop Stimulation: Out-of-Distribution Robustness
papers.summary: Brains and large language models need not be considered equivalent systems to reveal an interpretable commonality: both exhibit high-dimensional, nonlinear dynamics whose behavior can only be modeled imperfectly. This creates a shared challenge whenever we seek to intervene in their dynamics. A controller may either rely on a model identified around a particular operating regime and risk failure as the system moves away from that regime, or explicitly account for uncertainty and a changing internal state. Neurostimulation has confronted an analogous problem for decades. The limitations of fixed, open-loop stimulation have motivated closed-loop and state-dependent approaches that condition intervention on the ongoing state of the neural system. Inspired by this principle, we formulate LLM steering as a feedback-control problem in which the network's internal state, rather than a fixed intervention alone, determines how the system is perturbed. We further account for the mismatch between tractable dynamical models and the nonlinear transformer they approximate through robust control. As one principled realization of this framework, we develop an $H_\infty$-based steering controller that limits sensitivity to disturbances and linearization mismatches. Across multiple steering benchmarks, the controller improves performance over existing baselines, with particularly pronounced gains under out-of-distribution conditions and varying length complexities. Beyond controller performance, we introduce robust steerability, $S_{\mathrm{rob}}$, a pre-deployment measure of tolerance to dynamics mismatch; across model-task pairs, it exhibits task-specific structure and varies systematically with model scale. Beyond robust LLM steering, our measure asks not merely whether control is possible, but how much uncertainty it can survive; a principle that may span artificial and biological neural systems.

authors.name: Kasra Fallah, Rudramani Singha, Hannah Ghanei, Paul Sajda, James Anderson, Erfan Zabeh

papers.title: Modeling Gene Expression Noise: From Transcriptional Dynamics to Cell Growth and Division
papers.summary: Gene expression is inherently noisy, leading to substantial cell-to-cell variation in mRNA and protein levels. The telegraph model and the simpler bursty model provide good fits to single-cell count distributions and have been used extensively to understand transcriptional kinetics and estimate the kinetic parameters. However, these models all describe a static cell. Here, we review models of stochastic gene expression in growing and dividing cells which aim to understand how a cell's own life history, from its birth, through copying its genome, to its division, leaves a distinct fluctuation signature on molecule numbers. We discuss the biochemical and biophysical processes captured by these models, their analytical tractability, the concept of cyclo-stationary behavior, when this is well approximated by the steady-state of static models and how the distributions of molecular numbers measured under these conditions sensitively depend on the experimental setup. This is followed by a discussion of how these models are fitted to single-cell measurements, how biological variability can be separated from measurement noise, and which computational advances make this feasible for thousands of genes. We finish by highlighting the open problems in the field.

authors.name: Augustinas Sukys, Lucy Ham, Kaan \"Ocal, James Holehouse, Ramon Grima

papers.title: Learning Time-Varying Connectomes for Stable Behavior Across Development
papers.summary: Neural circuits must maintain functionality to drive effective behavior while their size, topology, geometry, and intrinsic dynamics change across development. To model developing visuomotor circuits and behavior, we investigated whether a single compact generative encoding could produce functional recurrent controllers across such changes. Building on the HyperNEAT algorithm, we represented this program as a compositional pattern-producing network that received developmental time as an input to generate age-specific connectivity. The developmental substrate prescribed neuronal birth, position, sensory organization, and intrinsic time constants. We tested this approach using two geometrically distinct developmental substrates and two visuomotor tasks: optomotor responses and phototaxis. Controllers optimized at only the initial or mature substrate generally failed when evaluated at other ages. In contrast, controllers optimized across multiple developmental snapshots maintained substantially higher and more consistent performance across trained and unseen ages. Optimization at only three developmental snapshots was often sufficient to produce effective behavior across the tested developmental interval. The resulting connectomes changed substantially with age and did not converge on a single trajectory of sparsity or connection-weight statistics. Controllers also differed in whether they relied on neurons born later in development. These results demonstrate that a shared spatiotemporal time-varying connectivity program can produce recurrent neural networks that preserve behavior across substantial developmental changes. Together, these results provide a framework for studying how functional stability can emerge without requiring structural or dynamical stability.

authors.name: Christof Fehrman, Jacob J. Morra, Eva A. Naumann

papers.title: Fluctuations in Environmental Resource Availability Alter the Oscillatory Tragedy of the Commons
papers.summary: Environmental noise in real-world complex systems--including fluctuations in temperature, humidity, and related environmental conditions--inevitably modulates individual metabolic capacity and, consequently, the efficiency of public-resource utilization. Yet conventional evolutionary game models incorporating environmental feedback treat resource dynamics deterministically. Here, we incorporate stochastic fluctuations into a noise-corrected replicator-dynamics framework. Theoretical analysis and stochastic birth-death simulations yield a counterintuitive result: moderate environmental noise stabilizes, rather than destabilizes, the interior fixed point across diverse payoff landscapes, while suppressing or eliminating catastrophic oscillations. These findings reframe environmental variability not merely as a perturbation but as a mechanism that fosters strategy coexistence and sustainable resource use in complex social and ecological systems.

authors.name: Yi-Duo Chen, Zhi-Xi Wu, Jian-Yue Guan

papers.title: An Exact Poisson Mixture Representation of Siler Remaining Life Expectancy
papers.summary: The Siler model describes mortality from birth to old age as the sum of a declining immaturity hazard, a constant background hazard, and an increasing senescence hazard. No standard closed form is available for its remaining life expectancy, which must therefore be evaluated by numerical integration. We show that Siler remaining life expectancy at age $x$ is a Poisson mixture of Gompertz-Makeham remaining life expectancies, that is, a Poisson-weighted average of life expectancies in models with only a constant background hazard and an exponentially increasing senescence hazard. All components share the senescence hazard. Their background hazards increase from one component to the next by the rate at which immaturity mortality declines. The Poisson mean is the immaturity hazard that remains to be accumulated after age $x$. This representation yields an exact series of generalized exponential integrals with a closed-form bound on the truncation error. Replacing the background hazard by its discounted counterpart also gives the Laplace transform of the remaining lifetime. The mixture bounds the life expectancy lost to immaturity mortality: up to a term below the reciprocal of $a_2+b_1$, this loss equals the probability of an immaturity death times the life expectancy with the immaturity hazard removed. In annual Siler fits to Swedish female mortality, we estimate that the loss at birth fell from 4.3 years in 1900 to less than 0.01 years in 2020, which accounts for 15% of the gain in life expectancy at birth over the period.

authors.name: Silvio C. Patricio

papers.title: Limited knowledge exchange across biological subfields in agent-based modelling: an LLM-assisted bibliometric analysis
papers.summary: Agent-based models (ABMs) are widely used across the biological sciences. While applications differ between biological subfields, the mathematical and statistical methods underlying ABMs largely do not, raising the question of how much knowledge is exchanged between subfields. We address this question by developing a bibliometric pipeline that combines a database keyword search with coarse- and fine-grained classification by a large language model (LLM). We apply the pipeline to the Web of Science Core Collection, classifying 22,936 ABM articles into ecology, epidemiology, oncology, other-biology, or not-biology. Using citation patterns and author overlap as proxies for knowledge exchange, we find that 83%, 81%, and 69% of citations from ecology, epidemiology, and oncology articles, respectively, go to articles in the same subfield. Furthermore, 91% of authors with at least two articles across these subfields publish exclusively within one subfield.
